Key Characteristics & Etiology: Systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica serovars Typhi or Paratyphoid A, B, C; transmitted via fecal-oral route through contaminated food/water.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Bacteria invade intestinal M cells of Peyer's patches, disseminate through mesenteric lymph nodes into thoracic duct, causing secondary bacteremia and reticuloendothelial seeding.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), rose spots on abdomen, hepatosplenomegaly, pea-soup diarrhea or constipation; Red flags: intestinal perforation, GI hemorrhage.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Blood culture (gold standard 1st week); stool/urine culture (2nd-3rd week); Widal test (O & H titers); Primary Rx: IV Ceftriaxone or oral Azithromycin (due to fluoroquinolone resistance).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute secretory diarrheal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae (serogroups O1 and O139); transmitted by fecal-oral contamination of water supplies.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Cholera toxin (AB toxin) binds GM1 ganglioside, irreversibly activates adenylate cyclase, elevating intracellular cAMP and causing massive hypersecretion of water and electrolytes into gut lumen.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Profuse painless 'rice-water' liquid stools, fishy odor, projectile vomiting, severe dehydration (sunken eyes, washerwoman hands, loss of skin turgor), hypovolemic shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Darkfield microscopy (darting motility); stool culture on TCBS agar; Primary Rx: Aggressive oral rehydration therapy (ORS) or IV Ringer's Lactate; adjunctive Azithromycin or Doxycycline.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica following ingestion of mature quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated food/water.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Trophozoites invade colonic mucosa, creating classic 'flask-shaped' ulcers; hematogenous spread via portal circulation to liver causes liquefactive necrosis (amoebic liver abscess).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Dysentery with blood and mucus, abdominal colic, tenesmus; Liver abscess: RUQ pain, high fever, right shoulder pain, hepatomegaly; 'Anchovy sauce' brown pus on aspiration.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Stool microscopy (E. histolytica cysts/trophozoites with ingested RBCs); stool antigen/PCR; USG/CT abdomen for liver mass; Rx: Oral Metronidazole/Tinidazole followed by luminal agent (Paromomycin/Diloxanide furoate).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute intestinal infection caused by Shigella species (S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, S. sonnei); highly contagious via fecal-oral route with low infectious dose (10-100 organisms).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Invades colonic epithelial cells, inducing intracellular replication and cell-to-cell spread; S. dysenteriae type 1 produces Shiga toxin, causing mucosal microvascular damage and HUS.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: High fever, severe abdominal cramps, tenesmus, frequent small-volume stools with frank blood, pus, and mucus; Red flags: Toxic megacolon, Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Stool microscopy (abundant PMNs and RBCs); stool culture on MacConkey/XLD agar; Primary Rx: Rehydration + Ciprofloxacin, Azithromycin, or Ceftriaxone.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Mosquito-borne protozoal infection transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes; caused by Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, or P. malariae.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Sporozoites infect hepatocytes (forming hypnozoites in vivax/ovale); merozoites invade RBCs causing synchronous hemolysis; P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) causes cytoadherence and microvascular sequestration.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Paroxysmal fever with chills/rigors, diaphoresis, splenomegaly, anemia, jaundice; Severe/Cerebral Malaria (P. falciparum): impaired consciousness, seizures, ARDS, severe anemia, hemoglobinuria (blackwater fever).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Giemsa-stained thick (sensitivity) and thin (species identification) blood films; Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs for PfHRP-2); Rx: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT e.g. Artemether-Lumefantrine); IV Artesunate for severe malaria; Primaquine for relapse prevention (vivax/ovale after G6PD check).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Arboviral infection caused by Dengue Virus (serotypes DENV 1-4) transmitted by Aedes aegypti / Aedes albopictus mosquitoes.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Secondary infection with different serotype causes antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), triggering massive inflammatory cytokine release, endothelial dysfunction, and severe capillary permeability.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden high fever ('breakbone fever'), severe retro-orbital headache, myalgias, arthralgias, maculopapular rash, positive tourniquet test; Severe Dengue: plasma leakage, pleural effusion/ascites, severe bleeding, dengue shock syndrome (DSS).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: NS1 antigen ELISA (days 1-5); IgM/IgG serology (after day 5); CBC (leukopenia, progressive thrombocytopenia, rising hematocrit indicating plasma leakage); Rx: Isotonic fluid management; Avoid NSAIDs/Aspirin due to bleeding risk.

Entity / Condition: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO) & Neutropenic Fever
Key Characteristics & Etiology: PUO: Fever > 38.3 C on multiple occasions for > 3 weeks without diagnosis. Neutropenic Fever: Fever >= 38.3 C with ANC < 500 cells/uL in oncology patients.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: In neutropenia, absence of mature neutrophils prevents normal localized inflammatory response, allowing minor mucosal translocation of pathogens to rapidly progress to fulminant bacteremia.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Persistent unexplained fever, rigors, mucositis, subtle catheter site erythema; Red flags: septic shock, rapid hemodynamic instability.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Blood cultures x 2 sets (peripheral and central lines), CBC with differential, CRP, CXR, urinalysis; Neutropenic Fever Rx: Immediate empiric broad-spectrum anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (Piperacillin-Tazobactam or Cefepime IV) within 1 hour.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV-1/2) infection transmitted via sexual contact, blood exposure, or vertical transmission.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Viral gp120 binds CD4 molecule and CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptors, infecting and destroying CD4+ T helper lymphocytes, causing progressive cellular immune deficiency.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Acute HIV syndrome (fever, LAD, rash); Asymptomatic phase; AIDS (CD4 < 200/uL): opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia / PCP, Cryptococcal meningitis, CNS Toxoplasmosis, esophageal candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: 4th generation HIV 1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay; confirmatory HIV-1 RNA PCR; CD4 count & viral load monitoring; Primary Rx: Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART: 2 NRTIs + 1 NNRTI/INSTI e.g. Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir); Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 < 200.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae; affects skin, peripheral nerves, and upper respiratory tract mucosa.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Cell-mediated immune response dictates spectrum: Tuberculoid (strong Th1 immunity, localized hypopigmented anesthetic plaques) vs Lepromatous (weak immunity, diffuse nodular skin lesions, high bacterial burden).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesions with loss of sensation, thickened peripheral nerves (ulnar, common peroneal), claw hand, foot drop, leonine facies, painless trophic ulcers.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Slit-skin smear for Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB / Fite-Faraco stain); skin biopsy; Primary Rx: WHO Multidrug Therapy (MDT) — Paucibacillary (Rifampicin + Dapsone for 6 months), Multibacillary (Rifampicin + Dapsone + Clofazimine for 12 months).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Rabies: Lyssavirus transmitted via saliva from infected animal bite (dogs, bats). Tetanus: Clostridium tetani exotoxin (tetanospasmin) from soil-contaminated wounds.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rabies virus travels retrograde via peripheral nerves to CNS causing encephalitis; Tetanospasmin retrogradely migrates to spinal cord, inhibiting Renshaw cell GABA/glycine release causing trismus and spasms.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Rabies: Hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, hypersalivation, fatal encephalopathy; Tetanus: Trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, painful muscle spasms, opisthotonos.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): Thorough wound washing with soap & water for 15 min + Rabies Vaccine (days 0, 3, 7, 14) + Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltrated into wound; Tetanus: Wound debridement + Tetanus Toxoid booster + Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG) for dirty wounds.
